> **Proposed API.** New conversion and authoring helpers follow
> `docs/api-vision.md`; they are not implemented here. Code blocks are static
> design examples, not executed or validated results.

An easier R interface must not make JSON less precise. An empty object, an
empty array, a missing field and an explicit `null` are different data. A
large integer must not change because it crossed into an ordinary R vector.

The proposed interface makes those boundaries easier to express, not easier
to ignore.

```r
library(lm15)
```

## Construct a shape or convert existing data explicitly

Use constructors when writing a small object directly:

```r
payload <- json_object(
  label = "example",
  values = json_array(1L, 2L),
  note = NULL
)
```

Use conversion helpers when you already have R data:

```r
object <- as_json_object(list(label = "example", note = NULL))
array <- as_json_array(c("Montreal", "Oslo"))

as_json(object)
as_json(array)
```

`as_json_object()` requires an explicitly named list with unique string keys.
`as_json_array()` accepts an unnamed list or a plain unnamed vector and makes
its array meaning explicit. Named input must first be deliberately stripped
of names by the caller; names are never silently discarded.

Empty conversions still have distinct meanings:

```r
as_json(as_json_object(list()))  # {}
as_json(as_json_array(list()))   # []
as_json(json_object(note = NULL))  # {"note":null}
```

The comments show the intended JSON shapes, not captured output.

JSON keys are not R variable names. The proposal allows an explicitly supplied
empty-string key and does not repair punctuation or spaces:

```r
keys <- setNames(list(1L, "kept"), c("", "not an R name"))
as_json(as_json_object(keys))
```

Duplicate keys and missing names are errors. There is no `make.names()` step,
no automatic factor/date conversion, and no guessing of shape during
serialization.

## Omit optional fields, not the contents of a payload

A typed value omits its own empty optional fields. Opaque payloads—data owned
by the application or provider—keep their contents exactly.

```r
as_json(config())
as_json(config(store = FALSE))
as_json(text(""))

call <- tool_call_part(
  "call_1", "lookup",
  input = json_object(query = "", filters = json_object(), ids = json_array(), note = NULL)
)
as_json(call)
```

`FALSE` is a real setting. An empty text part is still text. Empty values inside
`call$input` are not clutter for an outer serializer to remove.

```r
saved <- as_json(call)
restored <- from_json(saved, kind = "part")
```

The `kind` selects an lm15 type family, not a provider. Reading then writing
this value should preserve its canonical meaning. A JSON Schema embedded in a
tool declaration is likewise a payload, not an invitation to rewrite schema
keywords to please one server.

## Keep three input boundaries distinct

**Constructors** are the preferred way to author new requests. Unknown argument
names and invalid values raise useful R input errors.

**Canonical readers** retain the shared contract's forward compatibility:
ordinary unknown fields may be ignored, while unknown content discriminators
are refused. A separate authoring check can catch field-name mistakes before
using that reader:

```r
json <- '{"max_tokens":20,"temperature":0.2}'
settings <- json |>
  check_canonical_fields(kind = "config") |>
  from_json(kind = "config")
```

`check_canonical_fields()` returns the original input invisibly on success.
It checks field names at typed nodes, not arbitrary keys inside a tool input
or schema. Value and type checks still belong to construction/deserialization.
It does not silently change the default reader into a stricter one.

**Foreign-format import**, such as `request_from_openai_chat()`, has a different
job: every provider-format key needs a mapping, explicit passthrough, or
refusal. Its behavior must not be weakened to match canonical-reader leniency.

## Let the field decide its number type

```r
as_json(config(max_tokens = 20, temperature = 1L))
```

`max_tokens` is an integer field; `temperature` is a floating-point field.
Supplying an integral value of the other R number type is fine. Supplying a
fractional token limit is not. `TRUE` does not become `1`.

For an integer too large for ordinary R numbers, supply its digits as text
before R can round them:

```r
large <- integer_value("9007199254740993")
as_json(usage(input_tokens = large, output_tokens = 2L))
as_json(large + 2L)
```

This remains an exact scalar value, not a promise that every base R vector or
summary operation supports arbitrary-size integers. The proposal provides
clear display and explicit conversions rather than an incomplete numeric
vector type.

## Choose how to interpret a parsed numeric token

Opaque JSON numbers retain their original tokens. Use a named conversion when
an application needs a number for computation:

```r
call <- from_json(
  '{"type":"tool_call","id":"c","name":"count","input":{"n":9007199254740993,"weight":0.25}}',
  kind = "part"
)

n <- json_number_integer(call$input$n)
weight <- json_number_double(call$input$weight)
```

The integer conversion refuses fractional values instead of rounding.
The double conversion explicitly chooses ordinary finite floating-point
arithmetic, but refuses an integral token beyond the safe integer range.
Neither conversion changes `call$input`.

For tables, `usage_dbl()` is the checked numeric view and `usage_chr()` is the
exact decimal-text view. Unknown counts remain missing in both.

## Choose the scope of provider-data serialization

```r
answer <- response(
  "demo-model", message_assistant("hello"), "stop",
  provider_data = json_object(example_metadata = "provider-owned")
)

as_json(answer)
as_json(answer, include_provider_data = TRUE)
responses_json(list(answer, NULL), include_provider_data = TRUE)
```

The last call returns one JSON array string and keeps the NULL position.
The inclusion policy is applied to each response separately. It does not
become a recursive cleanup rule for arbitrary nested data.

An inclusion option supplied on an incompatible root should be rejected, not
silently ignored. Use the collection writer when you mean a collection of
responses. Existing type-specific rules for nested canonical values remain
part of the contract.

Provider data can contain sensitive or large content. Automatic printing
never dumps it; explicit serialization is an application decision.

## Describe media before resolving its source

```r
image <- image_part(url = "https://example.org/photo.png", media_type = "image/png")
document <- document_part(path = "report.pdf", media_type = "application/pdf")

bytes <- charToRaw("small local payload")
binary <- binary_part(data = bytes, media_type = "application/octet-stream")
media_bytes(binary)
```

Each part has one source. Constructing URL/path values does not fetch or read
them. `media_bytes()` is an explicit request for local bytes: it decodes inline
data or reads a local path, but does not quietly fetch URL/file-ID content.
Request preparation may resolve local paths when an operation needs them.

A valid part is not a promise that every provider accepts it. Unsupported media
or settings still cause a refusal. Preserve returned parts and continuation
state when replaying a conversation rather than reconstructing them from text.
